title: Confucius and the Good Person
objective: After this level you can explain Confucius's ideal of the junzi, the exemplary person, and his ideas of ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety).
summary: Confucius made the junzi a person of moral nobility, not noble birth, marked by ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety) done with real feeling; the Mohists attacked costly rituals.

cards.headline: Born noble, or become noble?
cards.body: In early China, the word Confucius built his ethics on first meant someone with the right parents. He helped make it mean someone with the right character.

cards.headline: The exemplary person
cards.body: Confucius (traditionally 551 to 479 BCE) comes down to us mainly through the Analects, a collection of his sayings and conversations. Its ideal is the junzi. The word originally meant “prince’s son”. Confucius helped turn it into a title of moral nobility, open to someone from any background. Early English translators wrote “gentleman”; some now prefer “exemplary person”. You can’t inherit it. You have to earn it.

cards.headline: Ren: humaneness
cards.body: The broadest Confucian virtue is ren, translated humaneness, benevolence or simply goodness. The same shift happened here. Before Confucius, ren described the strong, handsome look of an aristocrat. In the Analects it’s a moral excellence anyone can reach, summed up once as “caring for others”.

cards.headline: Li: ritual with feeling
cards.body: Asked about ren, Confucius spoke of overcoming yourself and returning to li, ritual propriety: the rites and etiquette of life, down to what to wear. But he had no patience for empty form. He said he couldn’t bear ritual without reverence, or mourning without grief. At a funeral, the mourners’ distress matters more than the formalities. Li is kindness that shows up on time and dressed properly.

cards.headline: The Mohist complaint
cards.body: Not everyone agreed. The Mohists, followers of the thinker Mozi, attacked the lavish funerals and long mourning the Confucians promoted. Their argument: such customs bring poverty, fewer people and disorder, so a truly benevolent person would cut them back. Both sides claimed to be the ones really caring for others.

cards.headline: Confucius and the Good Person: the big picture
learned: Junzi: moral nobility, not noble birth
Li: ritual and etiquette, done with feeling

questions.prompt: What did Confucius help turn the word junzi into?

options.label: A title only a prince’s son could hold
A title of moral nobility anyone could earn
The name of a court ritual
A word for a wandering hermit

questions.explanation: Junzi first meant “prince’s son”; Confucius helped make it a title of moral nobility open to people of any background.

questions.prompt: What did Confucius think was wrong with performing a ritual perfectly but without feeling?

options.label: Nothing, as long as every step was correct
options.rationale: He couldn’t bear ritual without reverence.

options.label: Rituals should be replaced by written laws
Ritual needs real feeling, like grief at a funeral
Only rulers were allowed to feel during rituals

questions.explanation: Confucius said he couldn’t bear ritual without reverence or mourning without grief; the mourners’ distress matters more than formalities.

questions.prompt: Level 1 said philosophy began in more than one place. Which Greek thinker lived within a few centuries of Confucius?

options.label: Galileo
options.rationale: He lived about two thousand years later.

options.label: Andronicus of Rhodes
options.rationale: He edited Aristotle’s books much later.

questions.explanation: Thales in Greece, Confucius in China and the Buddha in India all lived within a few centuries of one another.
